intro_en: The Israel National Trail passes gradually from the Judean Desert and the Dead Sea Rift to the Negev. We start in the Dead Sea Rift and part from it on a gentle climb up Ma'ale Tzurim to Ramat Mazar and Har Tzurim. The trail passes above the Peres pools (Gevei Peres) and the waterfall beside them; at the point where Nahal Peres enters the canyon, it is recommended to descend to the pools and the head of the waterfall. It's worth it!
character_en: Most of the route is on dirt roads. Ma'ale Tzurim is comfortable and gentle, and there is one more short climb up to Road 25 at the end of the route
transport_en: There is no access to the starting point. The nearest bus stop to the end point is at HaArava Junction, about 10 km from the Nahal Tamar campsite
important_en: When crossing Nahal Azgad there is a danger of mines at the sides of the road. Walk only on the road and do not cross fences.
In summer 2017 Nahal Ashalim was contaminated by gypsum effluent that leaked from a breached reservoir. As of the time of publication: entry to the upper stream is prohibited.
At the Nahal Tamar overnight campsite there is no drinking water; the nearest resupply point is the petrol station at HaArava Junction.
description_en:
The route begins at the overnight campsite on the Amiaz Plain, and proceeds west along a black-marked road. The road descends and crosses Nahal Amiaz. On the other side of the stream we pass a pumping facility of the Dead Sea Works. The Dead Sea Works pump brackish water from boreholes in the stream channels of the area, and it is used for the industrial activity at the plants.
After a short walk we reach a trail junction, where the Israel National Trail turns left together with the red marking. The black-marked road climbs to the right up to the desert plateau: Ma'ale Azgad.
We cross Nahal Azgad and after it the channel of Nahal Ashalim. The trail continues to another trail junction: the red-marked road heads east to Road 90, and the Israel National Trail continues south with a blue-marked road.
We pass under the potash conveyor of the Dead Sea Works, a large conveyor belt that carries the potash from the Dead Sea Works up to the Rotem Plain, a distance of 18 km and an elevation difference of 800 metres. Potash is the main product extracted from the Dead Sea water, through a process of evaporation. In addition to potash, bromine and magnesium are also produced. Potash is used mainly as fertiliser in agriculture, supplying plants with the element potassium, an element also essential to animals, including humans, who obtain it by eating plants.
On the way south, we walk among marl badlands at the foot of the cliff, and cross several channels and tributaries, including the streams Nahal Hamrit and Nahal Admon.
At the entrance to Ma'ale Tzurim, the marking colour changes from blue to red, and the trail turns right, leaves the dirt road and begins to climb.
In the first part of the climb, the trail ascends over rock steps until it turns right towards the north-west. From here we climb along the route of the historic Ma'ale Tzurim. The Arabic name of the ascent, Naqb al-Buwaib, meaning 'the ascent of the gates', hints that we are probably not the first to climb it. The ascent is gentle and comfortable, and it appears that in the past someone laboured, built and hewed along it to prepare it as a convenient passage between the Negev Highlands and the Sodom Plain (Kikar Sdom), on foot and perhaps even on pack animals. A passage cut into the rock at the top of the ascent is an example of this preparation work.
At the top of the ascent is Mitzpe Tzurim, with a beautiful view to the east. We can see the evaporation ponds of the Jordanian and Israeli Dead Sea works. Beyond the ponds, in Jordanian territory, we can see where Wadi Hasa, thought by some to be the biblical Zered Brook, emerges from the mountains into the Dead Sea Rift. North of the wadi are the Mountains of Moab and south of it the Mountains of Edom. Near the outlet lies the Jordanian town of As-Safi, south of which some identify the location of the city of Zoar, mentioned in the Bible in connection with Abraham, Lot and Sodom.
The trail continues on a vehicle track. At the junction with a black-marked road, we turn left towards the south, across the desert plateau. Beside the trail we can see several surfaces covered with carpets of dark stones: hamadas, flint stones or stones coated with patina, a dark coating on the surface of the stones.
The trail turns west, and ahead of us we can see slopes and a high ridge line, the continuation of the Hatzera Ridge, in which the Small Crater (Makhtesh Katan) was formed, extending north to the Nahal Heimar area.
We are in the transition zone between the Judean Desert and the Negev. The desert plateau on which the trail runs and the fault escarpment to the east are two landscapes typical of the Judean Desert. In contrast, west of us is a ridge that characterises the geology and topography of the Negev. The boundary between the Judean Desert and the Negev is not sharp enough to be marked as a clear line on the map; it is gradual, and geographers debate where exactly it should be drawn in the area between Nahal Zohar and Nahal Ashalim.
After a short distance we reach a trail junction: the Israel National Trail continues to the right, alongside the red and green markings, while a green-marked road turns left.
It is recommended to leave the trail and descend from the junction to the Peres pools (Gevei Peres) and to the lookout from the head of the waterfall: at the junction we turn left, and after a short walk descend right into the channel, to the pools among the pale rock surfaces. In winter the pools are usually full, but there is no need to pass through the water. It is also worth approaching, carefully, the head of the waterfall, below which large boulders lie scattered in disarray, like a toppled tower of blocks. Before returning to the trail, it is worth spending a little more time exploring the three arms of the canyon, to the waterfalls and pools at the head of the gorge.
From the junction where the Israel National Trail turns right, we proceed, bypass the gorge and continue south on a dirt road with red marking. After a short distance, the Israel National Trail and the red marking leave the dirt road, climb right to a saddle and 'cut' a bend that the road makes.
After the trail crosses the dirt road on the other side of the saddle, it descends to Nahal Tahmas. We cross the stream and climb up to Road 25, the Dimona - HaArava Junction road. At the top of the climb, the trail turns right and proceeds parallel to the road along a row of electricity poles, as far as the entrance to the dirt road that leads to the gate of the Small Crater.
We cross the road and proceed along a red-marked road. This is our entry into an area that until a few years ago was a phosphate mine of ICL, the company that operates the phosphate mines in the Negev. When mining ended, ICL carried out rehabilitation works in this area in an attempt to restore it, as far as possible of course, to its original topography before mining. The lookout point we pass was also built as part of the rehabilitation project. It is worth going in to the lookout and reading the signs that explain about the surroundings, the mining and the rehabilitation.
A little after the lookout point, the Israel National Trail turns right off the dirt road into a small valley; on the other side of the valley there are convenient flat areas for those wishing to set up for an overnight camp.
Points of interest: the potash conveyor. Ma'ale Tzurim. The Peres pools (Gevei Peres).
Recommended lodging in the area
Ein Gedi Field School
author_en: Itzik Ben Dov, Trail Marking Coordinator, Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel (SPNI).
